pregabalin.name: Pregabalin
pregabalin.summary: Pregabalin is a prescription medicine used for nerve pain, epilepsy and generalised anxiety disorder. It most often causes sleepiness, dizziness and headaches. Some people can become addicted to it, and in the UK it is a controlled medicine.
usedFor: Nerve (neuropathic) pain, including pain from damaged nerves
pregabalin.howItWorks: For epilepsy, pregabalin is thought to reduce abnormal electrical activity in the brain. For nerve pain, it is thought to block pain by interfering with pain messages travelling through the brain and down the spine. For anxiety, it is thought to stop the brain from releasing the chemicals that make a person feel anxious. MedlinePlus places pregabalin in a group of medicines called anticonvulsants.
pregabalin.onset: The NHS says it takes at least a few weeks for pregabalin to work.

common: The NHS says the most common side effects are feeling sleepy, feeling dizzy and headaches.
The NHS says these side effects are usually mild and go away by themselves.
NHS trust leaflets list vision disturbances, indigestion, weight gain, leg swelling, tremor and tiredness as other possible effects.
serious: The NHS describes a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) as rare, and lists swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or struggling breathing, as signs to call 999.
The NHS lists hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there) as a reason to call a doctor or NHS 111 now.
Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust notes that a few people taking pregabalin have had suicidal thoughts, which can happen after only a week of treatment.
For thoughts of harming oneself or ending one's life, the NHS lists 999 or A&E; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123, which is free at any time, can also help.
The NHS says to go to A&E now after taking more than the prescribed amount if there is sleepiness, confusion, agitation, a seizure or fainting.
The MHRA says pregabalin has been linked to infrequent reports of severe breathing difficulty (respiratory depression), including some cases in people not taking opioids.
The MHRA says gabapentin and pregabalin can cause potentially fatal respiratory depression, particularly when used with opioid medicines and alcohol.
The NHS says some people can become addicted to pregabalin, and that the dose is reduced gradually when stopping to avoid withdrawal symptoms.
The NHS says not to stop pregabalin without talking to the doctor.

cautions: The NHS lists groups who may not be able to take pregabalin, including people who have had an allergic reaction to it, who have ever misused or been addicted to a medicine, or who have breathing problems, heart disease, or liver or kidney disease.
The NHS says pregabalin in pregnancy is usually only advised if a doctor thinks the benefits outweigh the possible risks, and suggests talking to a doctor or pharmacist before breastfeeding.
Some brands of pregabalin liquid may contain sodium, so people on a controlled-sodium diet are advised to check first.
A Dudley NHS leaflet advises against driving when feeling drowsy.
The NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol, because it may cause sleepiness or poor focus.
The NHS says pregabalin can intensify the highs of heroin and other opioids.

The MHRA lists compromised breathing, respiratory or neurological disease, kidney impairment, other medicines that depress the central nervous system, and older age as higher risk for severe breathing difficulty.
The NHS says pregabalin does not stop any type of contraception working, except that severe diarrhoea lasting more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills.
pregabalin.monitoring: The MHRA advises prescribers to assess people for a history of drug abuse before prescribing pregabalin, and to observe them for signs of abuse and dependence. The NHS says blood sugar may need to be checked more often in the first few weeks for people with diabetes.

sections.heading: What is pregabalin used for?
sections.body: Pregabalin is a prescription medicine used to treat nerve pain, epilepsy and generalised anxiety disorder. Nerve pain, also called neuropathic pain, is pain from damaged nerves. The NHS says nerve pain can be caused by different conditions, such as diabetes and shingles. MedlinePlus says pregabalin is used to relieve neuropathic pain, including pain from diabetes and the pain that can follow shingles. The NHS lists the brand names Alzain, Axalid, Lyrica and Misabri. MedlinePlus places pregabalin in a group of medicines called anticonvulsants. GOV.UK says pregabalin became a Class C controlled drug in April 2019, and that it is illegal to possess it without a prescription or to supply it to others. The NHS says pregabalin comes as capsules, tablets and a liquid to drink.

sections.heading: How does pregabalin work?
sections.body: The NHS describes how pregabalin works as a theory that differs by condition. For epilepsy, pregabalin is thought to reduce abnormal electrical activity in the brain. For nerve pain, it is thought to block pain by interfering with pain messages travelling through the brain and down the spine. For anxiety, it is thought to stop the brain from releasing the chemicals that make a person feel anxious. One NHS trust leaflet notes that it is not fully understood how pregabalin works. The NHS says it takes at least a few weeks for pregabalin to work. Pregabalin and gabapentin are often grouped together as gabapentinoids. The NHS says gabapentin is thought to work in a similar way for epilepsy and nerve pain. MedlinePlus places pregabalin in a group of medicines called anticonvulsants.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of pregabalin?
sections.body: The NHS says the most common side effects of pregabalin are feeling sleepy, feeling dizzy and headaches. It says these are usually mild and go away by themselves. NHS trust leaflets list vision disturbances, indigestion, weight gain, leg swelling, tremor and tiredness as other possible effects. A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare, and the NHS lists swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or struggling breathing, as signs to call 999. The NHS lists hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there) as a reason to call a doctor or NHS 111 now. A few people taking pregabalin have had suicidal thoughts, which can happen after only a week of treatment. For thoughts of harming oneself or ending one's life, the NHS lists 999 or A&E; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time, can also help. The NHS says not to stop pregabalin without talking to the doctor.

sections.heading: Dependence, misuse and stopping pregabalin
sections.body: The NHS says some people can become addicted to pregabalin. It also says that when stopping, the dose is reduced gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms, and that pregabalin should not be stopped without talking to the doctor. GOV.UK says pregabalin and gabapentin became Class C controlled drugs, and Schedule 3 under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, from 1 April 2019. It says it is illegal to possess them without a prescription and illegal to supply or sell them to others. The MHRA advises prescribers to assess people for a history of drug abuse before prescribing pregabalin and gabapentin. It also advises observing people for signs of abuse and dependence. The MHRA says these medicines can cause drowsiness, sedation and potentially fatal respiratory depression, particularly when used with opioid medicines and alcohol. The NHS also says pregabalin can intensify the highs of heroin and other opioids.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with pregabalin?
sections.body: The NHS lists groups who may not be able to take pregabalin, including people who have had an allergic reaction to it, have ever misused or been addicted to a medicine, or have breathing problems, heart disease, or liver or kidney disease. The NHS says pregabalin in pregnancy is usually only advised if a doctor thinks the benefits outweigh the possible risks, and suggests talking to a doctor or pharmacist before breastfeeding. The MHRA lists compromised breathing, respiratory or neurological disease, kidney impairment, other medicines that depress the central nervous system, and older age as higher risk for severe breathing difficulty. The NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol, because it may cause sleepiness or poor focus. A Dudley NHS leaflet advises against driving when feeling drowsy. The NHS says pregabalin does not stop any type of contraception working, except that severe diarrhoea lasting more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills.

faqs.q: Is pregabalin addictive?
faqs.a: The NHS says some people can become addicted to pregabalin. It also says anyone who has ever misused or been addicted to a medicine may not be able to take it. The MHRA advises prescribers to assess for a history of drug abuse before prescribing. The NHS says not to stop pregabalin without talking to the doctor.

faqs.q: Is pregabalin a controlled drug?
faqs.a: GOV.UK says pregabalin and gabapentin became Class C controlled drugs, and Schedule 3 under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, from 1 April 2019. It says it is illegal to possess them without a prescription and illegal to supply or sell them to others.

faqs.q: Can pregabalin be stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS says that when stopping pregabalin the dose is reduced gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms. It also says not to stop pregabalin without talking to the doctor. The prescriber decides how to reduce the dose.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with pregabalin?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol with pregabalin, because it may cause sleepiness or poor focus. The MHRA says the risk of potentially fatal respiratory depression is greater with alcohol and opioid medicines. MedlinePlus also advises not drinking alcohol while taking pregabalin.

faqs.q: Does pregabalin affect driving or contraception?
faqs.a: Pregabalin can make a person sleepy or dizzy, and a Dudley NHS leaflet advises against driving when feeling drowsy. The NHS says pregabalin does not stop any type of contraception working, except that severe diarrhoea lasting more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills.

sections.heading: What is gabapentin used for?
sections.body:
Gabapentin is a prescription medicine that is used to treat epilepsy and nerve pain. The NHS says nerve pain can be caused by conditions such as diabetes and shingles, or by an injury. MedlinePlus, a United States health information site, says gabapentin is used together with other medicines to help control certain types of seizures in people with epilepsy. It also says gabapentin is used for the pain that can follow shingles, called postherpetic neuralgia. MedlinePlus adds that the medicine may help to control a condition but does not cure it.

Gabapentin comes as capsules, tablets and a liquid that is swallowed. It is available on prescription. The NHS says it is generally suitable for adults and for children aged 6 and over, and that a specialist sometimes prescribes it for younger children. The NHS also says people who take medicines for epilepsy are entitled to free prescriptions for all the medicines they take, not just the epilepsy ones.

sections.heading: How does gabapentin work, and what happens if it is stopped?
sections.body:
In epilepsy, the NHS says gabapentin is thought to calm abnormal electrical activity in the brain. For nerve pain, it is thought to act on pain signals in the brain and spine. The NHS says it takes a few weeks for gabapentin to work fully, and that seizures or pain may still happen during this time.

When gabapentin is stopped, the NHS says the dose is reduced gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms. It lists agitation or anxiety, panic attacks, palpitations (feeling the heartbeat) and difficulty sleeping among the withdrawal symptoms. MedlinePlus says that in people taking gabapentin for seizures, suddenly stopping the medicine may lead to seizures happening more often. The NHS says gabapentin can be taken with or without food.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of gabapentin?
sections.body:
The NHS says most people who take gabapentin do not get any side effects. Some people feel sleepy, tired and dizzy. Other common side effects listed by the NHS are feeling sick, swelling, blurred vision, dry mouth and weight gain. These common side effects are usually mild and go away by themselves. The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using machinery until a person feels better if they are sleepy or dizzy.

A few people taking gabapentin have had thoughts of harming themselves or ending their life, sometimes after only a week. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E straight away if this happens. For urgent mental health advice, NHS 111 (mental health option) can be called, and Samaritans are free to call on 116 123 at any time. A serious allergic reaction is rare. MedlinePlus lists difficulty breathing and swelling of the mouth, face, lips or tongue as signs, and these need emergency help by calling 999. The NHS also says to go to A&E or call 999 straight away if someone has taken more than the prescribed amount and feels dizzy or sleepy, has double vision, has slurred speech or faints.

sections.heading: Is gabapentin a controlled drug, and what about misuse and dependence?
sections.body:
Since 1 April 2019, gabapentin has been a controlled drug in Great Britain. GOV.UK says it was placed in Class C of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and in Schedule 3 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. GOV.UK says the change reflected growing concern about abuse. The NHS says there are strict rules on how gabapentin is prescribed and supplied, to make sure it is not given to the wrong person or misused.

The NHS says some people can become addicted to gabapentin. It lists people who have misused or been addicted to a medicine among those who should check with a doctor before taking it. The NHS says gabapentin can strengthen the effects of recreational drugs such as heroin and other opioids. It also says that taking gabapentin with recreational drugs raises the chance of unpleasant effects such as panic attacks, anxiety and memory loss. In an emergency, such as taking more than the prescribed amount, the NHS says to go to A&E or call 999.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about other medicines?
sections.body:
The NHS says people who have had an allergic reaction to gabapentin or another medicine should check with a doctor first. It also lists people with kidney problems or with lung conditions such as COPD or severe asthma. Gabapentin liquid contains sodium and potassium, so the NHS says people on a controlled sodium or potassium diet should check first. The NHS says gabapentin is not generally recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough information about its effects on the baby. It says a person can take gabapentin while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy, after talking to a doctor or pharmacist.

Antacids can reduce how much gabapentin the body takes in, and the NHS says to take them at least 2 hours apart. Strong painkillers such as morphine can make a person very tired and dizzy when starting gabapentin, according to the NHS. The NHS says there is not enough information to say that herbal remedies are safe to take with gabapentin. It adds that remedies which cause drowsiness could add to the side effects. The NHS says a person can drink alcohol while taking gabapentin, but it may make them feel sleepy or tired. It suggests it may be best to avoid alcohol in the first few days.

faqs.q: Can gabapentin be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says gabapentin is not generally recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough information about its effects on the baby. A person who is pregnant or trying for a baby is advised to check with a doctor first. The NHS says gabapentin can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy, after talking to a doctor or pharmacist.

faqs.q: Can you drink alcohol with gabapentin?
faqs.a: The NHS says a person can drink alcohol while taking gabapentin, but it may make them feel sleepy or tired. It suggests it may be best to avoid alcohol in the first few days of treatment. The NHS also advises against driving, cycling or using machinery until a person feels better if they are sleepy or dizzy.

faqs.q: Can gabapentin be stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS says that when gabapentin is stopped, the dose is reduced gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms. MedlinePlus says that in people taking gabapentin for seizures, suddenly stopping the medicine may lead to seizures happening more often.

faqs.q: Is gabapentin addictive?
faqs.a: The NHS says some people can become addicted to gabapentin. GOV.UK says that since April 2019 it has been a controlled drug in Great Britain, in Class C and Schedule 3, because of growing concern about abuse. The NHS says there are strict rules on how it is prescribed and supplied.

faqs.q: How long does gabapentin take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says it takes a few weeks for gabapentin to work fully. Most people who take it do not get side effects, and the NHS says the common ones are usually mild and go away by themselves.

duloxetine.name: Duloxetine
duloxetine.summary: Duloxetine is an antidepressant medicine that is also used for anxiety and nerve pain. It is taken as capsules and is only available with a prescription. The NHS lists very low mood with suicidal thoughts among its serious side effects; the routes to help are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123.
duloxetine.class: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) antidepressant
usedFor: Neuropathic pain in adults, where NICE says duloxetine is one of four medicines to offer first (not for trigeminal neuralgia)
duloxetine.howItWorks: Duloxetine is a serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, or SNRI. SNRIs are thought to work by increasing the amount of the mood-enhancing chemicals serotonin and noradrenaline in the brain.
duloxetine.onset: The NHS says duloxetine usually takes 2 to 4 weeks to work, and it may take longer when used for nerve pain. Some people feel worse during the first few weeks of treatment before they begin to feel better.

common: Headaches, feeling or being sick, dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth, diarrhoea or constipation, trouble sleeping, sexual problems and weight loss are listed by the NHS as common.
The NHS says not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery while feeling dizzy.
serious: Very low mood with suicidal thoughts is on the NHS list of serious side effects. For thoughts of ending life the NHS says call 999 or go to A&E now; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) are other routes.
A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is a rare serious effect, and the NHS says to call 999 immediately.
Unexplained muscle pain or weakness is listed by the NHS as a serious side effect, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected.
Serotonin syndrome causes a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaking, twitching muscles and feeling confused or agitated, and is on the NHS list of serious side effects.
Constant headaches, long-lasting confusion or weakness, or frequent muscle cramps can be signs of low sodium in the blood, and NHS 111 is the NHS route for suspected serious side effects.

Yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin can be a sign of a liver problem, although this may be less obvious on brown or black skin; the NHS advises contacting the GP urgently or calling NHS 111.
Black or red stools, or blood in vomit, can be signs of bleeding from the gut, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected.

cautions: The NHS lists an allergic reaction to duloxetine or another medicine, kidney or liver problems, a heart problem, glaucoma, a history of seizures, manic episodes or bipolar disorder, and bruising easily as reasons for the prescriber to take care.
The NHS says not to take the herbal remedy St John's wort during treatment with duloxetine because it raises the risk of side effects.
Warfarin and other blood-thinning medicines, and some older antidepressants called MAOIs, are among the medicines the NHS lists as needing care with duloxetine.
Tramadol can increase the chance of certain side effects when taken with duloxetine, the NHS says.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk but may make a person feel sleepy or tired, and it may be best to avoid it for the first few days until the effect is known.
MedlinePlus says alcohol can increase the risk of serious side effects.

The NHS says duloxetine is not generally recommended in pregnancy because there is little information on whether it may affect the developing baby, but if it was working well before pregnancy it may be reasonable to keep taking it.
Taking duloxetine in the last month of pregnancy may slightly increase the risk of bleeding after delivery, the NHS says.
The NHS says that if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, duloxetine can be taken while breastfeeding.
duloxetine.monitoring: MedlinePlus advises having blood pressure checked before starting treatment and regularly while taking duloxetine. It also suggests talking to the doctor about an eye examination before starting. The NHS says that a person who is not feeling any better after 6 weeks can talk to the doctor.
duloxetine.regimenNote: Duloxetine comes as capsules that the NHS says are swallowed whole, and the prescriber decides the dose, which depends on the condition being treated.

sections.heading: What is duloxetine used for?
sections.body:
Duloxetine is an antidepressant medicine that is also used for anxiety and nerve pain. It is only available with a prescription. The NHS describes duloxetine as an SNRI antidepressant. It is prescribed for depression and anxiety. It is also used to treat nerve pain, such as fibromyalgia. The NHS says it can be used to treat stress urinary incontinence in women. Most adults aged 18 years and over can take duloxetine, according to the NHS.

NICE guidance on neuropathic pain in adults says amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin should be offered as the initial treatment, except for trigeminal neuralgia, which is handled separately. Neuropathic pain is the medical name for nerve pain.

sections.heading: How does duloxetine work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
SNRIs are thought to work by increasing the amount of the mood-enhancing chemicals serotonin and noradrenaline in the brain. The NHS says duloxetine usually takes 2 to 4 weeks to work, and it may take longer if it is taken for nerve pain. Some people feel worse during the first few weeks of treatment before they begin to feel better. The NHS says that a person who is not feeling any better after 6 weeks can talk to the doctor.

Duloxetine comes as capsules, and the NHS says they are swallowed whole and not chewed. The NHS says the capsules can be taken with or without food. The dose depends on the condition being treated, and the prescriber decides it. Once someone is feeling better, the NHS says it is likely that they will keep taking duloxetine for several more months. If someone has been feeling better for 6 months or more, the NHS says the doctor may suggest coming off duloxetine.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, feeling or being sick, dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth, diarrhoea or constipation, trouble sleeping, sexual problems and weight loss as common side effects. It says not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery while feeling dizzy. The NHS also says duloxetine can sometimes cause more serious side effects, although most of them are rare.

Its list includes a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), unexplained muscle pain or weakness, serotonin syndrome and very low mood with suicidal thoughts. Serotonin syndrome causes a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaking, twitching muscles and feeling confused or agitated. Constant headaches, long-lasting confusion or weakness, or frequent muscle cramps can be signs of low sodium in the blood. Yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin can be a sign of a liver problem, although this may be less obvious on brown or black skin. Black or red stools, or blood in vomit, can be signs of bleeding from the gut. The NHS says to call NHS 111 if someone taking duloxetine thinks they may be having serious side effects, and to call 999 for a severe allergic reaction.

sections.heading: Mood, suicidal thoughts and stopping duloxetine
sections.body:
The NHS says some people feel worse during the first few weeks of treatment before they begin to feel better. The NHS lists very low mood with suicidal thoughts among the serious side effects, and for thoughts of ending life it says to call 999 or go to A&E now. If someone is in immediate danger, calling 999 or going to A&E is advised; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time, are other routes.

The NHS says antidepressants are not addictive, but withdrawal symptoms can occur if they are stopped suddenly or a dose is missed. For duloxetine, the NHS says the doctor will probably recommend lowering the dose gradually over several weeks to help prevent withdrawal side effects. Withdrawal symptoms listed by the NHS include dizziness, feeling sick, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, trouble sleeping, feeling agitated or anxious, headaches and shaking.

sections.heading: Taking duloxetine with other medicines, herbal products or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says not to take the herbal remedy St John's wort during treatment with duloxetine because it raises the risk of side effects. It says there is not enough information about other herbal remedies and supplements. Warfarin and other blood-thinning medicines, and some older antidepressants called MAOIs, are among the medicines the NHS lists as needing care with duloxetine. The NHS says tramadol can increase the chance of certain side effects. The NHS suggests telling the doctor or pharmacist about all medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins and supplements before starting.

The NHS says alcohol can be drunk but may make a person feel sleepy or tired. It may be best to avoid alcohol for the first few days, until it is clear how duloxetine affects the person. MedlinePlus says alcohol can increase the risk of serious side effects.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care?
sections.body:
The NHS lists an allergic reaction to duloxetine or another medicine, kidney or liver problems, a heart problem, glaucoma, a history of seizures, manic episodes or bipolar disorder, and bruising easily as reasons for the prescriber to take care. MedlinePlus advises having blood pressure checked before starting treatment and regularly while taking duloxetine. It also suggests talking to the doctor about an eye examination before starting.

The NHS says duloxetine is not generally recommended in pregnancy because there is little information on whether it may affect the developing baby. If it was working well before pregnancy, the NHS says it may be reasonable to keep taking it, and the doctor discusses the risks and benefits. Taking duloxetine in the last month of pregnancy may slightly increase the risk of bleeding after delivery. The NHS says that if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, duloxetine can be taken while breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Is duloxetine addictive?
faqs.a: The NHS says antidepressants are not addictive, but withdrawal symptoms can occur if they are stopped suddenly or a dose is missed. For duloxetine, the doctor will probably recommend lowering the dose gradually over several weeks to help prevent withdrawal side effects. The NHS advises talking to the doctor before stopping an antidepressant.

faqs.q: How long does duloxetine take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says duloxetine usually takes 2 to 4 weeks to work, and it may take longer if it is taken for nerve pain. Some people feel worse during the first few weeks of treatment before they begin to feel better. A person who is not feeling any better after 6 weeks can talk to the doctor, the NHS says.

faqs.q: Can duloxetine be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says duloxetine is not generally recommended in pregnancy because there is little information on whether it may affect the developing baby. If it was working well before pregnancy, it may be reasonable to keep taking it, and the doctor discusses the risks and benefits. The NHS says that if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, it can be taken while breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking duloxetine?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk but may make a person feel sleepy or tired. It may be best to avoid alcohol for the first few days, until it is clear how the medicine affects the person. MedlinePlus says alcohol can increase the risk of serious side effects.

faqs.q: What help is there if low mood or suicidal thoughts get worse?
faqs.a: Very low mood with suicidal thoughts is on the NHS list of serious side effects of duloxetine. For thoughts of ending life the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E now. If someone is in immediate danger, calling 999 or going to A&E is advised; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time, are other routes.

faqs.q: Is duloxetine only used for depression?
faqs.a: No, the NHS says duloxetine is prescribed for depression and anxiety, and also used to treat nerve pain such as fibromyalgia. It can be used to treat stress urinary incontinence in women. NICE lists duloxetine as one of four medicines to be offered first for neuropathic pain in adults, apart from trigeminal neuralgia.

sections.heading: What is venlafaxine used for?
sections.body: Venlafaxine is an antidepressant medicine. It belongs to a group called serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, or SNRIs, and it is used to treat depression. It is available only on prescription. Serotonin and noradrenaline are chemical messengers in the brain, and SNRIs are thought to work by raising their levels. The NHS and MedlinePlus say it may take several weeks or longer to feel the full benefit. UK product information lists standard tablets as well as prolonged-release tablets and capsules, which release the medicine slowly. The NHS says venlafaxine is not suitable for everyone, and it lists diabetes, epilepsy, heart problems, glaucoma and a bleeding disorder among the conditions that call for extra care. An earlier allergic reaction to venlafaxine is another reason it may not be suitable.

sections.heading: How is venlafaxine taken and stopped?
sections.body: The NHS says venlafaxine is usually taken with food. For a person who has trouble sleeping, the NHS says the morning is the best time to take it. MedlinePlus says a missed dose is taken once it is remembered, unless it is almost time for the next one, and that doses are not doubled up. The NHS adds that an alarm can help if doses are often forgotten. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, although the NHS says venlafaxine is not addictive. The NHS says a person who wants to stop should speak to the doctor first. The doctor will usually lower the dose gradually over several weeks or months, and this can take longer after long-term use. Stopping too early can also let depression come back.

sections.heading: What side effects can venlafaxine cause?
sections.body: Headaches, sweating and a dry mouth are among the common side effects. The NHS says most side effects should ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine. It says headaches usually go away after the first week, and that a dry mouth which does not go away after a week or two is worth raising with the doctor. If dizziness or drowsiness occurs, the NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery until it has gone away. The NHS says that anyone taking venlafaxine who thinks they may be having serious side effects can call NHS 111. It lists the signs of serotonin syndrome as a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaking, twitching muscles and feeling confused or agitated. The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or there is difficulty breathing, which can be signs of a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).

sections.heading: Low mood, self-harm and urgent help
sections.body: The NHS says it is uncommon, but some people have suicidal thoughts or an urge to self-harm when they start an antidepressant. People aged 24 or under, or who have had these thoughts before, may be most at risk. The NHS says to contact a GP, or go to A&E, for thoughts of killing or harming oneself at any time during treatment. If a person is in danger or cannot keep themselves safe, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, the NHS points to NHS 111 (mental health option). The Samaritans on 116 123 are free to call at any time. The NHS also suggests that telling a relative or close friend about starting an antidepressant can help them notice changes in behaviour.

sections.heading: Venlafaxine and blood pressure
sections.body: Venlafaxine can raise blood pressure. UK product information says dose-related rises in blood pressure are common, and that severe rises needing immediate treatment have been reported since the medicine came on the market. It says patients should be screened for high blood pressure and that existing high blood pressure should be controlled before treatment starts. It also says blood pressure should be reviewed periodically, after treatment starts and after dose increases. The US label describes dose-related rises in blood pressure and recommends regular blood pressure monitoring. UK patient leaflets ask people with a history of high blood pressure, heart problems or an abnormal heart rhythm to talk to their doctor before starting. The NHS says venlafaxine can make the heart beat faster or cause an irregular heartbeat. It also says some rarely used antidepressants can affect venlafaxine and cause very high blood pressure.

sections.heading: Other medicines, alcohol and pregnancy
sections.body: The NHS advises against using the herbal supplement St John's wort with venlafaxine because it raises the risk of side effects. UK patient leaflets say monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), another type of antidepressant, must not be taken with venlafaxine, and they ask people who have taken one recently to tell their doctor. The NHS lists anti-inflammatory painkillers such as aspirin and ibuprofen, and anticoagulants such as warfarin and apixaban, among medicines that may not mix well with it. Some UK leaflets name tramadol, triptans for migraine and dextromethorphan, found in some cough medicines, as examples that raise the risk of serotonin syndrome. The NHS says alcohol may make a person feel sleepy, and its main venlafaxine page says it is best not to drink because alcohol can raise the risk of side effects. The NHS says pregnancy and breastfeeding call for a discussion of the risks and benefits with the doctor.

faqs.q: Is venlafaxine addictive?
faqs.a: The NHS says venlafaxine is not addictive. However, withdrawal effects can happen if it is stopped suddenly. The NHS says a doctor will usually lower the dose gradually over several weeks or months. A person who wants to stop is advised to speak to the doctor first.

faqs.q: Does venlafaxine raise blood pressure?
faqs.a: UK product information says dose-related rises in blood pressure are common with venlafaxine. The US label recommends regular blood pressure monitoring. UK patient leaflets ask people with a history of high blood pressure or heart problems to talk to their doctor before starting. The NHS says anyone who thinks they may be having serious side effects can call NHS 111.

faqs.q: How long does venlafaxine take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS and MedlinePlus say it may take several weeks or longer to feel the full benefit. The NHS says most side effects should ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine. Stopping too early can let depression come back. The NHS says a person who wants to stop should speak to the doctor first.

faqs.q: Can alcohol or driving be a problem with venlafaxine?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol may make a person feel sleepy while taking venlafaxine, and its main venlafaxine page says it is best not to drink because alcohol can raise the risk of side effects. The NHS suggests it might be best to avoid driving and cycling for the first few days of treatment, until a person knows how the medicine makes them feel. If dizziness or drowsiness occurs, the NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery until it has gone away.

faqs.q: Can venlafaxine be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says pregnancy and breastfeeding call for a discussion of the risks and benefits with the doctor.

faqs.q: What if an antidepressant brings thoughts of suicide or self-harm?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is uncommon, but some people have suicidal thoughts or an urge to self-harm when they start an antidepressant. People aged 24 or under, or who have had these thoughts before, may be most at risk. The NHS says to contact a GP, or go to A&E, for such thoughts at any time during treatment, and to call 999 or go to A&E if in danger or unable to keep safe. NHS 111 (mental health option) and the Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time, are other routes to urgent support.

mirtazapine.name: Mirtazapine
mirtazapine.summary: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant, prescribed mainly for depression and sometimes for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and anxiety. The NHS says it is not a sleeping tablet but it can make people feel sleepy. The NHS says anyone with thoughts of harming themselves or ending their life should call 999 or go to A&E.
usedFor: Depression, which the NHS gives as the main reason it is prescribed
Sometimes obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and anxiety
mirtazapine.howItWorks: The NHS says mirtazapine works by increasing the amount of two mood-related chemicals in the brain, noradrenaline and serotonin. Pharmacology reviews describe it as blocking alpha-2 receptors on nerve cells, which increases noradrenaline and serotonin release, and as also blocking 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 serotonin receptors. Blocking histamine H1 receptors is linked to its sedating effect. Unlike many antidepressants, it is described as not inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline or serotonin.
mirtazapine.onset: The NHS says an improvement may be seen after a week, although it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to feel the full benefits.

common: Feeling drowsy or sleepy, headaches and a dry mouth are common side effects, the NHS says.
Increased appetite and weight gain, dizziness or shakiness, feeling or being sick, and diarrhoea are also listed by the NHS as common.
The NHS says the common side effects are usually mild and go away after a couple of weeks.
If sleepy, the NHS advises against driving or using machinery until a person feels fully alert.
For dry mouth the NHS suggests sugar-free gum or sweets.
serious: Thoughts of harming oneself or ending life: the NHS side effects page says to call 999 or go to A&E now, while the main NHS mirtazapine page says to call NHS 111 for these thoughts or any other serious side effect.
Samaritans can be reached free on 116 123 at any time, and calling NHS 111 and choosing the mental health option connects to someone trained to help with an urgent mental health crisis.
Signs of infection such as a high temperature, sore throat and mouth ulcers could be due to a problem with the blood cells, the NHS says, and it advises calling NHS 111 or a doctor.
The manufacturer's UK leaflets advise stopping mirtazapine and seeing a doctor for a blood test if signs of infection such as unexplained fever, sore throat and mouth ulcers appear.
Liver problems, where the whites of the eyes or the skin turn yellow, are listed by the NHS as a serious side effect, and it advises calling NHS 111.
Mania, feeling unusually high or full of energy, is also listed by the NHS as a serious side effect.
A serious allergic reaction is possible, and the NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, breathing becomes very fast or difficult, or the throat feels tight.

A manufacturer's UK leaflet says mirtazapine, alone or combined with certain other medicines, can lead to serotonin syndrome, with signs such as unexplained fever, sweating, a faster heartbeat, diarrhoea and muscle contractions. MedlinePlus, a US source, advises calling a doctor right away for fever, sweating, confusion or a fast or irregular heartbeat.

cautions: The NHS says mirtazapine is not usually recommended for anyone under 18.
The NHS says it may be unsuitable for people with liver, kidney or heart disease, epilepsy, diabetes or schizophrenia, or who have had an allergic reaction or serious side effect with it before.
The NHS says St John's wort should not be taken during treatment because it increases the risk of side effects.
The NHS says mirtazapine can affect warfarin, so the dose of warfarin may need to change.
The NHS says carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampicin can reduce the effect of mirtazapine, so a higher dose may be prescribed.
The NHS lists opioids such as morphine and medicines containing buprenorphine among the medicines to check before combining with mirtazapine.
The NHS lists methadone, stimulants such as MDMA and cocaine, and hallucinogens such as LSD as combinations that can be dangerous, and says cannabis can make a person very sleepy.
The NHS says alcohol can increase the risk of side effects such as feeling very drowsy.

The NHS says there is no good evidence that mirtazapine taken in early pregnancy affects a baby's development, and that taking it late in pregnancy may slightly raise the risk of bleeding after delivery.
The NHS says mirtazapine can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy, because it passes into breast milk in small amounts.
The NHS says there is no clear evidence that mirtazapine affects fertility in men or women.
The NHS says stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, and a doctor will probably recommend reducing the dose gradually.

sections.heading: What is mirtazapine used for?
sections.body:
Mirtazapine is an antidepressant. The NHS says it is prescribed mainly for depression, and sometimes for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and anxiety. UK product information shows it as tablets, as tablets that melt on the tongue, and as an oral solution.

The NHS says mirtazapine is not usually recommended for anyone under 18. It says it is not a sleeping tablet, but it can make people feel sleepy, which may help people with depression who struggle to sleep.

The NHS groups antidepressants into types such as SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs, and lists mirtazapine as a noradrenaline and specific serotonergic antidepressant, or NaSSA. The NHS says an improvement in symptoms may be seen after a week, although it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to feel the full benefits. A prescriber is the person to talk to about whether this medicine suits someone.

sections.heading: How does mirtazapine work?
sections.body:
The NHS says mirtazapine works by increasing the amount of two mood-related chemicals in the brain, noradrenaline and serotonin. Pharmacology reviews describe it as blocking alpha-2 receptors on nerve cells, which increases the release of noradrenaline and, through further receptors, serotonin. They add that it also blocks 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 serotonin receptors, which is linked to its calming and anti-sickness effects.

This pattern is why mirtazapine is called a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant, or NaSSA. Unlike many other antidepressants, it is described as not inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline or serotonin.

Blocking histamine H1 receptors is linked to its sedating effect and to increased appetite. The NHS says mirtazapine is not a sleeping tablet but can make people feel sleepy. Because of this, the NHS advises against driving or using machinery until a person feels fully alert.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of mirtazapine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists feeling drowsy or sleepy, headaches and a dry mouth as common side effects. Increased appetite and weight gain, dizziness or shakiness, feeling or being sick, and diarrhoea are also listed. The NHS says these are usually mild and go away after a couple of weeks. For dry mouth, it suggests sugar-free gum or sweets.

Serious side effects are rare. The NHS lists allergic reaction, thoughts of suicide or self-harm, mania, liver problems and signs of infection from blood cell problems. The NHS describes the signs of infection as a high temperature, sore throat and mouth ulcers, and advises calling NHS 111 or a doctor. UK leaflets advise a prompt blood test if these signs appear.

The NHS side effects page says to call 999 or go to A&E now if a person has thoughts of harming themselves or ending their life, while the main NHS page says to call NHS 111. NHS 111 has a mental health option, and Samaritans can be reached free on 116 123 at any time.

sections.heading: Taking mirtazapine with other medicines, alcohol or drugs
sections.body:
The NHS says St John's wort should not be taken during treatment because it increases the risk of side effects. It says mirtazapine can affect warfarin, so the dose of warfarin may need to change. It says carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampicin can reduce the effect of mirtazapine. It also lists opioids such as morphine and medicines containing buprenorphine among those to check before combining.

The NHS says alcohol can increase the risk of side effects such as feeling very drowsy. It lists methadone, stimulants such as MDMA and cocaine, and hallucinogens such as LSD as combinations that can be dangerous, and says cannabis can make a person very sleepy. It adds that mirtazapine has not been properly tested with recreational drugs.

A manufacturer's UK leaflet says mirtazapine, alone or combined with certain other medicines, can lead to serotonin syndrome, with signs such as unexplained fever, sweating, a faster heartbeat, diarrhoea and muscle contractions. MedlinePlus, a US source, advises calling a doctor right away for fever, sweating, confusion or a fast or irregular heartbeat.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about stopping?
sections.body:
The NHS says mirtazapine may be unsuitable for people with liver, kidney or heart disease, epilepsy, diabetes or schizophrenia. It may also be unsuitable for people who have had an allergic reaction or serious side effect with it before.

The NHS says there is no good evidence that taking mirtazapine in early pregnancy affects a baby's development, and that taking it late in pregnancy may slightly raise the risk of bleeding after delivery. It says mirtazapine can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy, because it passes into breast milk in small amounts. It also says there is no clear evidence that mirtazapine affects fertility in men or women.

The NHS advises against stopping an antidepressant suddenly, because it can cause withdrawal symptoms. A doctor will probably recommend reducing the dose gradually. The NHS says that for a mental health crisis, 999 is the route if someone is in immediate danger, and NHS 111 has a mental health option.

faqs.q: Is mirtazapine a sleeping tablet?
faqs.a: The NHS says mirtazapine is not a sleeping tablet, but it can make people feel sleepy. The NHS advises against driving or using machinery until sleepiness has gone and a person feels fully alert.

faqs.q: How long does mirtazapine take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says an improvement in symptoms may be seen after a week. It usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to feel the full benefits. A person who feels no better, or has troubling side effects, can talk to the prescriber, because the choice of medicine is the doctor's to review.

faqs.q: Does mirtazapine cause weight gain?
faqs.a: The NHS lists increased appetite and weight gain as common side effects, and describes feeling like eating more than usual. It notes that the common side effects usually go away after a couple of weeks. A prescriber or pharmacist can discuss weight if it becomes a concern.

faqs.q: Can mirtazapine be taken with alcohol?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can increase the risk of side effects of mirtazapine, such as feeling very drowsy. It says cannabis can make a person very sleepy, and lists methadone, MDMA, cocaine and LSD as combinations that can be dangerous. A doctor or pharmacist can advise on individual circumstances.

faqs.q: What if mirtazapine brings thoughts of suicide or self-harm?
faqs.a: The NHS lists thoughts about suicide or self-harm among the serious effects. Its side effects page says to call 999 or go to A&E now if a person has thoughts of harming themselves or ending their life, while its main mirtazapine page says to call NHS 111. Samaritans can be reached free on 116 123 at any time, and NHS 111 has a mental health option.

faqs.q: Can mirtazapine be stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS says stopping an antidepressant suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms. A doctor will probably recommend reducing the dose gradually. The NHS says withdrawal symptoms are usually short-lived and often stop within a few weeks.

sections.heading: What is fluoxetine used for?
sections.body:
Fluoxetine is an antidepressant medicine, and the NHS lists depression, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and bulimia as the conditions it treats. The NHS says it can sometimes be used for menopause symptoms. MedlinePlus, a US source, names depression, OCD, some eating disorders and panic attacks, and says it relieves the symptoms of premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

The NHS depression guidance says fluoxetine is the only SSRI that can be prescribed for under-18s and, even then, only when a specialist has given the go-ahead. One NHS page says children aged 8 and older can take it for depression, while another says it is sometimes used for depression in children aged 5 or older. MedlinePlus says fluoxetine is approved to treat depression in teenagers and in children aged 8 and older. A Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent formulary document notes that prescribing under 8 years old is off label.

sections.heading: How does fluoxetine work, and why does it stay in the body?
sections.body:
Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, or SSRI, which is a type of antidepressant. SSRIs are thought to work by increasing the level of serotonin in the brain. The NHS advises giving fluoxetine at least 6 weeks to work.

Half-life is the time it takes for the amount of a medicine in the body to fall by half. US prescribing information says fluoxetine and its active breakdown product, norfluoxetine, have long half-lives. This means active drug stays in the body for weeks after dosing stops. The same labelling says several weeks should pass between stopping fluoxetine and starting an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor, a rarely used type of antidepressant) for this reason.

sections.heading: What are the serious side effects of fluoxetine?
sections.body: The NHS describes serious side effects of fluoxetine as uncommon. Serotonin syndrome is a serious side effect that causes a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaking, twitching muscles and confusion; the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, severe dizziness or fainting, or a fit. Unexplained bruising or bleeding from the gums should prompt a call to a doctor or NHS 111 straight away, according to the NHS. A serious allergic reaction, such as a swollen throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, needs a call to 999, the NHS says. Signs of low sodium levels, such as headaches, trouble concentrating, memory problems or confusion, are another reason the NHS gives for calling 999 or going to A&E. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for advice straight away after taking more than the prescribed amount of fluoxetine.

sections.heading: Thoughts of self-harm and where to get help
sections.body:
The NHS says thoughts of harming oneself or ending one's life are rare with SSRIs but can occur when treatment starts, and that people aged 24 or under may be at particular risk. If such thoughts occur at any time, the NHS says to contact the GP or go to hospital straight away, and to call 999 or go to A&E if in immediate danger. MedlinePlus says caregivers of teenagers should watch for suicidal thoughts or behaviours, and for worsening nervousness, irritability, moodiness or sleeplessness, and get medical help right away.

Free help is also available from Samaritans on 116 123, at any time, and from NHS 111 (mental health option). Samaritans says its helpline can be called free from any phone. The NHS also lists an emergency GP appointment, or the mental health crisis team for people who have one, as places to turn.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and coming off fluoxetine
sections.body:
Most adults can take fluoxetine, but the NHS says it is not suitable for everyone. The NHS advises checking first with a heart problem, epilepsy, electroconvulsive treatment, glaucoma, diabetes or a past episode of mania. A Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust leaflet on fluoxetine says it can change blood sugar levels, so people with diabetes may need to check their blood sugar more often.

The NHS says fluoxetine can be used in pregnancy if needed, and the doctor discusses the risks and benefits. The NHS says fluoxetine in pregnancy can sometimes cause short-term withdrawal symptoms in the newborn and, rarely, breathing problems. The NHS says fluoxetine can be taken while breastfeeding if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy.

The NHS says a course of SSRIs usually continues for at least 6 months after a person feels better, to prevent the condition coming back. The NHS says that if someone has felt better for 6 months or more, the doctor may suggest coming off fluoxetine. The NHS advises against stopping suddenly. After long-term use, a gradual reduction is usually recommended.

sections.heading: Alcohol and other medicines
sections.body:
The NHS fluoxetine page advises against drinking alcohol because it can raise the risk of side effects such as drowsiness, while another NHS page says alcohol can be drunk but may cause sleepiness and may be best avoided for the first few days.

The NHS lists MAOI antidepressants such as moclobemide and selegiline, anticoagulants such as warfarin and apixaban, and NSAIDs such as aspirin and ibuprofen among medicines that may not mix well with fluoxetine. The NHS advises against taking St John's wort with fluoxetine, because it raises the risk of side effects. The NHS says there is not enough information on other herbal remedies and supplements taken with fluoxetine. US prescribing information says several weeks should pass after stopping fluoxetine before an MAOI is started, because fluoxetine stays in the body.

gabapentinoids.name: Gabapentinoids
gabapentinoids.summary: Gabapentinoids are the group that contains pregabalin and gabapentin, which are used for epilepsy and nerve pain.
gabapentinoids.mechanism: For epilepsy, these medicines are thought to reduce abnormal electrical activity in the brain. For nerve pain, they are thought to block pain by affecting pain messages travelling through the brain and down the spine.
cautions: The NHS lists drowsiness and dizziness among the common side effects of both medicines.
The NHS says some people can become addicted to either medicine.
The NHS says that when stopping either medicine the dose is reduced gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

snris.name: SNRIs
snris.summary: SNRIs are a group of antidepressants whose NHS examples are duloxetine and venlafaxine. They act on both serotonin and noradrenaline. The NHS says venlafaxine is used to treat depression and sometimes anxiety and panic attacks, and duloxetine is used for depression, anxiety and nerve pain. NHS formulary guidance says venlafaxine and duloxetine can also increase heart rate and blood pressure.
snris.mechanism: SNRIs are thought to work by increasing the amount of the mood-enhancing chemicals serotonin and noradrenaline in the brain.
cautions: The NHS says antidepressants are not addictive, but withdrawal symptoms can occur if they are stopped suddenly or a dose is missed.
A Scottish NHS guide says venlafaxine carries a higher risk of withdrawal effects than other antidepressants.

NHS formulary guidance says venlafaxine and duloxetine can increase heart rate and blood pressure, and the NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service says they can cause dose-related rises in blood pressure and abnormal heart rhythms.
The routes to help for suicidal thoughts are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123.

noradrenergic-and-specific-serotonergic-.name: Noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressants (NaSSAs)
noradrenergic-and-specific-serotonergic-.summary: The NHS groups antidepressants into types such as SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs, and lists mirtazapine as a noradrenaline and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA). Mirtazapine is the NaSSA covered on this site.
noradrenergic-and-specific-serotonergic-.mechanism: Pharmacology reviews describe mirtazapine as blocking alpha-2 receptors on nerve cells in the brain, which increases the release of noradrenaline and serotonin, and as also blocking 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 serotonin receptors. Unlike many other antidepressants, it is described as not inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline or serotonin. Blocking histamine H1 receptors is linked to its sedating effect.
cautions: The NHS says mirtazapine is not usually recommended for anyone under 18.
The NHS says stopping an antidepressant suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, and the dose is usually reduced gradually.
The NHS says mirtazapine can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy.
